Article Title: ‘It could well be KL Rahul’: Ex-India cricketer on Delhi Capitals captaincy plans after Rishabh Pant trade
Article Text:
Delhi Capitals' Axar Patel and KL Rahul (PTI Photo)

Former India cricketer and commentator Aakash Chopra has flagged several concerns surrounding Delhi Capitals' preparations for the upcoming IPL season following their trade for Rishabh Pant from Lucknow Super Giants. While the franchise has strengthened its batting options, Chopra believes uncertainty over the captaincy and questions surrounding the pace-bowling department could pose significant challenges.The biggest question, according to Chopra, is who will lead Delhi. With Pant and KL Rahul among the potential candidates, the franchise still appears to have a decision to make. Chopra also suggested that Axar Patel may not be keen on taking up the leadership role, making Rahul a possible frontrunner.“There are multiple questions, actually. It’s an MCQ because who will be the captain? Rishabh Pant has been a captaincy candidate, KL Rahul is an option, and I’m hearing that Axar doesn’t want to be the captain. So, with everything going on, you don’t even know who will captain the side. It could well be KL Rahul at this stage,” Chopra told JioStar.Chopra also underlined the importance of getting Pant's batting position right. Having brought the wicketkeeper-batter back through a trade, Delhi must ensure that he gets an opportunity in the top four rather than being pushed down the order. He felt that failing to do so would prevent the franchise from making full use of Pant's abilities.Chopra also believed Lucknow may have come out better from the exchange, given the quality of bowler they received in Kuldeep Yadav.“And Rishabh Pant, now that you have traded him, must bat in the top four. If you are going to bat him lower than that, then you will not utilise him to his fullest potential. I felt that in that trade, LSG was better off because you couldn’t have asked for more than a bowler of Kuldeep’s calibre for that pitch,” he added.While Delhi have assembled a formidable batting lineup, Chopra feels their bowling resources could be a major area of concern. The uncertainty surrounding Mitchell Starc 's availability is one of the factors, with the franchise potentially having to reassess its pace-bowling combinations depending on the Australian's participation.He also questioned the returns expected from Delhi's more expensive fast-bowling options, pointing out that Mukesh Kumar and Auqib Nabi command substantial investments, while Starc comes at an even higher price. In contrast, Lungi Ngidi proved to be an excellent bargain after being acquired for Rs 2 crore. Chopra also mentioned Dushmantha Chameera and Kyle Jamieson as relatively economical options.“Ashutosh, Sameer Rizvi, Tristan Stubbs , plus Axar Patel, and then you’ve got Miller. So, it’s a very decent setup. The problem area for them will be their bowling department. Because Mitchell Starc, will he play? It will be a conversation as to whether he will be available to play or not.They will face an issue with their fast bowling this season and how they plan to address it, I’ve got no idea.“Mukesh is at eight crore, Auqib Nabi at Rs 8.4 crore, and then you have Mitchell Starc at nearly 12, so that’s a lot of money. Lungi Ngidi was cheap, picked up for Rs 2 crore. He turned out to be a fantastic bargain. Dushmantha Chameera and Kyle Jamieson weren’t as expensive either. But the more expensive players might not be available. Their pedigree and current form are still uncertain, and Mukesh Kumar’s T20 numbers have actually plummeted a little,” Chopra stated.
Article Summary: Aakash Chopra has flagged several concerns surrounding Delhi Capitals' preparations for the upcoming IPL season. Chopra believes uncertainty over the captaincy and questions surrounding the pace-bowling department could pose significant challenges. The former India cricketer also underlined the importance of getting Rishabh Pant's batting position right.

Article Title: Sonia Gandhi memoir: The 1966 fight between Muhammad Ali and Henry Cooper that former Congress president remembers from her Cambridge days
Article Text:
When Ali floored Cooper in ‘moral victory’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Sonia and the '60s is also a tale of a young girl swept in the tide of civil rights blowing across the globe.In her memoir 'Belonging', mentioning Martin Luther King, "free speech movement" in Berkeley and students movements in Europe as the influences on her generation, the Congress matriarch has fleetingly, but noticeably, referred to an indelible episode from the timeless story of boxing great Muhammad Ali . This was among the "memorable moments" in Cambridge after Sonia met Rajiv Gandhi. On a May 1966 evening, Sonia and friends gathered at a friend's place glued to the radio to listen to "the blow-by-blow boxing match between Ali and British boxer Henry Cooper. "She adds, "when Clay beat Cooper in the sixth round of the match, we roared in triumph. It was for us not just a victory in a sport but a moral one as well. We had been roused by Martin Luther King Jr's massive demonstration in Washington and his 'I have a dream' speech."It was a momentous evening - not just for the prize fight - but for the times it represented. Two years ago, Ali had not only become the world heavyweight champion, acquired a reputation as a blabbermouth, but also a flaming rebel and a political lightening rod who shook the white establishment of Jim Crow America with his black pride assertion.A rebellion that would take him to oppose the draft to fight in the Vietnam War with that stinging barb - "I ain't got no quarrel with 'em VietCong".It led to his exile from boxing, before his return four years later shook the world more than his initial avatar, interspersed with gladiatorial battles like 'Rumble in the Jungle' and 'Thrilla in Manila'. But prior to Ali's exile were his two fights with Cooper, the British champion. The first was in 1963 as Cassius Clay, then still a braggard who backed his claims with heavy punches and floored opponents with blinding speed. Clay went to London in the hope of mopping up points to force the reigning heavyweight champion, the scary Sonny Liston to give him a chance at the title.This was the fight that is remembered for trainer Angelo Dundee's gamesmanship that saved the day for Clay and kept him in business for future. Who knows if it had turned out differently.Clay had mocked Cooper like he did to all - predicting to end it in five rounds. But 'Enry's 'Ammer', that dreaded left hook (hammer) that Cooper was famous for, put Clay on his backside in the fourth round. Ali later said, "it made me feel as if I had gone back and visited all my ancestors in Africa". It was enough, almost. But a small split in the seam of one glove, that trainer Angelo Dundee had seen before the fight but retained presciently for an emergency, was now put to good use .As Ali "slumped on his stool like a sack of potatoes", Dundee stuck his finger in the split and made it bigger and then asked the referee for a change of gloves. That earned Clay enough seconds to return to his senses. He recovered to batter Cooper. A year later, Clay shocked the world by defeating Liston twice, embraced Islam and became the most famous man on earth.As the heavyweight champion and a global icon, Clay returned to London as Ali for a 1966 rematch with Cooper. This was the phase when, along with protests, Malcolm X and King, Ali himself was the flush face of the fight for social justice.The bout itself, though, was an anticlimax. Unlike the heroic failure of the first fight, Cooper was no match this time. And the duel was stopped in the 6th round with Cooper bleeding profusely.And this was the outcome that Sonia and friends rejoiced over that evening, at a friend’s dig at Cambridge, as a “moral victory”.
Article Summary: The Congress matriarch has fleetingly, but noticeably, referred to an indelible episode from the timeless story of boxing great Muhammad Ali. This was among the "memorable moments" in Cambridge after Sonia met Rajiv Gandhi. On a May 1966 evening, Sonia and friends gathered at a friend's place glued to the radio to listen to the blow-by-blow boxing match between Ali and British boxer Henry Cooper.

Article Title: Rs 50 lakh debt, visa nightmare: Teenage Indian chess prodigy risks losing US scholarship
Article Text:
IM Md Imran (Special Arrangements)

The Bratislava incident that changed everything

A university dream on hold

A family stretched to its financial limits

A race against time

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

One final Grandmaster norm

El Llobregat Open, Spain: December 3 to 8

NEW DELHI: Last June, seventeen-year-old Md Imran was in Bratislava, Slovakia, when an incident turned his European chess campaign into a nightmare. As previously reported on TimesofIndia.com , he lost his passport, his phone, money and several personal belongings. More than just his valuables, he had lost something far more important, his valid US F-1 visa and Schengen visa.Stranded in a foreign country, with no easy way to get home or continue his journey, the young Indian chess player suddenly found himself fighting a battle that had little to do with the 64 squares. But Imran, hailing from Andhra Pradesh, refused to let the setback end his journey.In the days and weeks that followed, he produced two consecutive Grandmaster (GM) norms, bringing him within touching distance of the coveted Grandmaster title.Yet, four months after that incident, Imran is back in India, facing a different kind of situation, which includes an unresolved US visa crisis, mounting family debt, and the possibility of losing a full university scholarship that could change his life.The teenager, who became an International Master (IM) in 2025, has already deferred his admission to the University of Texas at Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) in Brownsville, Texas, from Fall 2026 to Spring 2027.His new university orientation is scheduled for January 19, 2027. If he cannot secure his US F-1 visa before then, he risks losing the scholarship altogether.For a teenager who has spent years travelling across continents to chase his Grandmaster dream, the next few months could prove decisive.The consequences of losing his passport in Bratislava were particularly severe because it contained both his valid US F-1 visa and his Schengen visa, which was valid until October 31.He eventually managed to obtain a replacement passport from the Indian Embassy in Budapest on June 29 and returned to India on July 6. But coming home did not mean the troubles were over."The very next day, on July 7th, I applied for a new Schengen visa for Hungary. This marked my 13th attempt at applying for a Schengen visa," Imran told TimesofIndia.com.Despite having competed extensively in Hungary over the previous two years, and having previously received a one-year multiple-entry visa from the same consulate, Imran was granted only a three-month visa, valid from July 18 to October 31.The decision left him frustrated, particularly when he knew fellow players who had received visas valid for two to five years in far fewer attempts."It sounded completely ridiculous, especially when I know many friends who have received 2- to 5-year validity visas in just their 2nd to 5th attempts. I truly don't understand what's wrong with my case," he added.For a young professional chess player, travelling back to India solely to process visas means more than another appointment and a few documents."Flying back to India solely for visa processing costs an exorbitant amount of time and heavy money on flight tickets, on top of the constant re-application hurdles," he added.Even amid the uncertainty, Imran had already earned two norms in closed round-robin tournaments and was chasing his final open Swiss GM norm to complete the requirements for the Grandmaster title.His original plan was to continue competing in Europe, secure the remaining norm and return to India in time to obtain a US visa and attend UTRGV's Fall 2026 student orientation on August 23. But the US visa appointment never materialised."I waited in Europe and tried for a U.S. appointment all the way through August, September, and October. Unfortunately, despite trying every single day for four months since the June incident, I still have not secured an appointment," he said.With the August university deadline passing, he had little choice but to defer his admission to Spring 2027.His scholarship remains at stake. If he cannot make it to the university by the January 19 orientation, he could lose the financial support that would help him pursue higher education alongside his chess career.Between July and October, he competed in over ten events. However, only three were strong open tournaments where he had a realistic opportunity to secure his final GM norm.The remaining events were regular prize-money opens and round-robin competitions that helped him stay active.The three major opportunities were also poorly spaced, with two tournaments scheduled back-to-back between August 8 and 23, followed by the final one from October 3 to 11.It was a relentless schedule, made even harder by the uncertainty surrounding his university admission and his inability to secure a US visa appointment.The pressure eventually took its toll on the chessboard."Under the intense psychological pressure of the missing norm and my crumbling U.S. visa situation, my performance dipped. I suffered an insane rating decline despite relentless fighting spirit. Completely exhausted and under immense stress, I flew back home on October 12," Imran, who had a peak rating of 2503 and is now rated 2477, revealed.Imran's father is a police officer, while his mother is a homemaker. Coming from a middle-class background, the family has had to stretch its resources to support his international chess career.Playing professionally in Europe costs between Rs 1.5 lakh and Rs 3 lakh every month. The expenses include flights, visas, accommodation, tournament entry fees, food and travel between countries.The family has reportedly accumulated loans of around Rs 40-50 lakh to finance his career. The June incident in Slovakia added another unexpected financial burden, with the loss of his passport, phone and other valuables."My father has supported me with everything he possibly can, stretching himself to the absolute limit, but it's falling short over time," Imran further noted. "I built my chess career entirely through my own hard work without formal high-end coaching."Imran has approached the Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister's Office and other political leaders, seeking financial assistance through state sports incentive schemes. However, his requests have so far gone unanswered.With his three-month Schengen visa approaching its October 31 expiry, Imran returned to the Hungarian Consulate in Mumbai on October 16 for another application. It was his 14th Schengen visa application.This time, he received an emergency appointment and was granted a one-year visa on October 24. While the longer validity offers some relief, it was still shorter than the five-year visa he had hoped to secure given his extensive tournament and travel history across Europe.At least one part of the travel crisis had eased. But the bigger problem remained untouched, his US F-1 visa. With January 19, 2027, approaching, Imran now needs to secure an appointment and complete the visa process in time to join UTRGV and protect his scholarship.Despite everything, Imran is preparing to return to Europe for another demanding tournament circuit in the hope of securing his final GM norm. He is scheduled to fly back on November 19, with four events lined up across Portugal, Spain and Sweden:The schedule leaves little room for rest. More importantly, he is desperately hoping to secure a US visa appointment before leaving India on November 19."My life is currently at a critical crossroads. Between the heavy financial debts of playing professional chess, the constant struggle to secure my final GM norm, and the looming threat of losing my U.S. university scholarship at the University of Texas at Rio Grande Valley if I can't resolve my visa crisis by Spring 2027, the situation is completely overwhelming," he concluded.For a teenager who has done so much to keep his dreams alive, the question is whether the support he needs will arrive before January 19.
Article Summary: Indian chess player Md Imran was in Bratislava, Slovakia, when an incident turned his European chess campaign into a nightmare. He lost his passport, his phone, money and several personal belongings. He also lost his valid US F-1 visa and Schengen visa. Four months after that incident, Imran is back in India, facing a different kind of situation, which includes an unresolved US visa crisis.

Article Title: A week without end for PT Usha: How a quiet rebellion derailed IOA president's second-term ambitions
Article Text:
PT Usha (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: PT Usha's second-term bid as Indian Olympic Association (IOA) president unravelled in 11 days, as a campaign for change within and outside the IOA gathered pace during her absence while she was in Dakar for the Youth Olympic Games (YOG), according to people familiar with developments. The week began on October 29. Usha met two influential political figures in Delhi, seeking their assurance and blessings for another term, sources said. At 7.09 pm, she filed her nomination for the Sportsperson of Outstanding Merit (SOM) election. That evening, she flew to Dakar for the YOG as part of the Indian delegation, with key office staff.After her departure, sources familiar with back-channel discussions alleged that those seeking a leadership change became active. Several calls, meetings in and outside Delhi and private message exchanges followed. As nominations deadline of Oct 30 passed, Usha's camp sensed alignments were shifting.The draft list, released the next day, deepened the unease. Usha was reportedly alerted in Dakar to a possible rebellion against her presidency. People close to her camp acknowledge that opposition had been building privately for four to five months.They say she was caught off guard and underestimated the challenge. Usha had planned to return on Nov 7. Developments prompted her to cut short the visit, sources said. Two scheduled International Olympic Committee (IOC) engagements kept her in the Senegal capital until Nov 2: a breakfast meeting with IOC vice-president Nawal El Moutawakel and four other delegates, followed by talks with IOC president Kirsty Coventry. They discussed India's 2036 Olympics bid and prospects of hosting the 2038 Asian Games. After the meetings, Usha booked a Nov 3 flight home, reached Delhi on Nov 4 morning and by noon, was present at the IOA office meeting with key aides. By then, mass withdrawals and changing positions among prospective SOM candidates had made her re-election prospects look uncertain, sources said.Sources alleged influential figures urged Usha to withdraw from the SOM contest. She declined, relying on assurances she believed she had received from her political bosses. She eventually lost by finishing fifth with 40 votes in a six-woman contest, possibly ending her bid for a second term as IOA president. Her backers concede she needed to be more proactive: the challenge had been taking shape while she was away.However, Usha separately wrote to electoral officer Sanjay K Srivastava to question an inclusion on the final SOM roster, allegedly of female SOM candidate Dola Banerjee's brother Rahul citing conflict of interest. It sought scrutiny of eligibility and inclusion or exclusion decisions, asking who authorised the inclusion of Rahul, under which rule and on what documentary basis, and whether a conflict of interest had been disclosed by Dola.Usha also filed four complaints with the electoral officer, in possession of TOI. They raised concerns over alleged requests for voters to confirm participation or provide proof of votes; messages invoking the sports ministry to seek voter confirmations; and WhatsApp appeals for a panel and four candidates, allegedly circulated by incumbent IOA executive committee members. She sought inquiry under Model Code of Conduct and ballot secrecy. Sources informed that Usha received no response from Srivastava till date.
Article Summary: PT Usha's second-term bid as Indian Olympic Association (IOA) president unravelled in 11 days. Campaign for change gathered pace during her absence while she was in Dakar for the Youth Olympic Games (YOG) Usha met two influential political figures in Delhi, seeking their assurance and blessings for another term, sources said.

Article Title: It is the responsibility of top athletes to look after the sports administration: Saina Nehwal
Article Text:
Saina Nehwal

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pune: London Olympics bronze medallistshuttler Saina Nehwal feels involvement of former top athletes in the administrative roles can lift the standard of Indian sports.The shuttler, who has won the Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) election of the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) polls, saids she feels the need to give it back to the sport. “It is a very good sign that sports is now being looked after by people who have played at the highest level. A lot of knowledge can be shared among these sportspersons, who come from different disciplines. Whatever knowledge I have gained from badminton, I will be able to share with theathletes, and similarly, I can learn from their experiences. We can collectively discuss what is required to build more champions and strengthen the sporting system in India,” she told TOI.“We have the Commonwealth Games coming up, and we are also looking at hosting the Olympics. Having experienced sportspersons in sports administration will only help improve our results and medal tally,” she said.Saina has won an Olympic medal and has recently retired from active badminton. She feels staying in touch with the sport makes it better for the administrators to understand the need of the sport better.“As you grow older, you begin to understand what it takes to make a champion and what all is required to achieve that.When I look at countries such as China and Korea, I notice that their sports associations are often headed by people who have themselves performed at the highest level and won Olympic medals. I strongly believe that experienced sportspersons who have performed at the highest level should be involved in every aspect of sports administration.They understand what is happening on the ground and what athletes actually need. They travel extensively with players and understand the challenges they face.”On the possibility of her contesting for the post of the president, she said, “I don't know. Whether it is me or any other sportsperson, it hardly matters. What matters is that we work together to improve Indian sport and increase our medal tally. We should aim to reach the level of countries such as China and America.The position of president or any other post will obviously have a name associated with it. But ultimately, the important thing is how we work together and what we can collectively achieve to win more medals for the country. ”
Article Summary: Saina Nehwal feels involvement of former top athletes in the administrative roles can lift the standard of Indian sports. The shuttler has won the Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) election of the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) polls.

NEW DELHI: New Zealand have been forced into another squad reshuffle ahead of the third ODI against India, with mounting injury concerns threatening to disrupt their plans for the remainder of the series.Fast bowler Kristian Clarke has been called up as cover for Blair Tickner ahead of Tuesday's third ODI, while Lockie Ferguson has been ruled out of the fourth and fifth matches after failing to recover fully from a calf injury sustained during the T20I series.The latest developments add to New Zealand's growing list of fitness concerns, with Matt Henry also recovering from a concussion-related issue and Tickner required to undergo a mandatory stand-down period despite being cleared of concussion.Ferguson has been ruled out of the final two ODIs after failing to recover fully from a low-grade tear in his right calf. The injury was sustained during the T20I series against India.Tickner, meanwhile, was struck by a ball while batting during the second ODI. Although he has since been cleared of concussion, his replacement in the playing XI by Matt Fisher means he must observe the ICC's mandatory seven-day stand-down period from the date of the match before returning to international cricket.Northern Districts fast bowler Clarke has consequently been drafted into the squad to provide additional bowling cover for the third ODI.Henry's availability also remains a concern. Initially cleared of concussion following his collision with Devon Conway in Auckland, the fast bowler was reassessed in Wellington and advised to target a return for the fourth ODI.New Zealand have also adjusted their plans for the transition from the ODI series to the upcoming Test assignment.Henry and Kyle Jamieson, who were initially scheduled to join the Test camp in Wellington after the third ODI, will now remain with the ODI squad for the fourth match.Two additional players are also expected to be brought into the squad across the fourth and fifth ODIs, with the composition for the final match still to be confirmed.Meanwhile, Tom Latham, Daryl Mitchell, Henry Nicholls, Glenn Phillips and Nathan Smith will leave for Wellington on Wednesday to begin preparations for the Test series. New Zealand Cricket said the Test squad to face India would be announced in the coming days.
Article Summary: New Zealand have been forced into another squad reshuffle ahead of the third ODI against India. Fast bowler Kristian Clarke has been called up as cover for Blair Tickner. Lockie Ferguson has been ruled out of the fourth and fifth matches after failing to recover fully from a calf injury. Matt Henry also recovering from a concussion-related issue.

Article Title: ‘Sacrifice runs for Virat Kohli’: Sunil Gavaskar's big take on pressure facing Shubman Gill and Shreyas Iyer
Article Text:
India's Virat Kohli

Mid-day

Poll Vote & Share your view Was Kohli's performance in the first ODI against New Zealand commendable? Yes, he played brilliantly. He could have done better. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Legendary India batter Sunil Gavaskar has weighed in on the debate surrounding Virat Kohli 's pursuit of 100 international centuries, suggesting that a teammate making a personal sacrifice to help the star reach the landmark would bring joy to Indian cricket fans as well.Kohli was in superb touch during the first ODI against New Zealand, smashing 74 off just 51 deliveries to guide India towards victory in a low-scoring contest. However, Gavaskar raised an interesting possibility in his latest column for: had Kohli stayed at the crease for longer, captain Shubman Gill and vice-captain Shreyas Iyer could have found themselves in a difficult position.With India closing in on the target, the two batters might have had to choose between finishing the match quickly and giving Kohli an opportunity to reach his century. The prospect becomes even more significant given that Kohli is chasing the historic mark of 100 international hundreds.Gavaskar acknowledged that winning a match must remain the team's primary objective, but argued that helping a player achieve such a landmark, provided it does not compromise the result, could be a moment of collective celebration."Indians have always been fond of records and so there's always a debate about the rights and wrongs of going for it.One thing for sure that 99% of those who say they don't play for records are actually incapable talent and temperament wise of setting any and so it's easy for them to say so," Gavaskar wrote."There is not a single Indian cricket fan who does not want Kohli to get to 100 international centuries. We are all cheering for him to get there and so, if there's an occasion where some other teammate sacrifices his runs to allow him the chance to get there, the glory will not be just Kohli's but for all Indian cricket fans too," he added.Kohli eventually fell for 74 with India at 124/3 in the rain-affected contest, leaving the team with relatively little work to do in the chase. His dismissal also meant Gill and Iyer did not have to confront the possibility of managing the chase around his personal milestone.Gavaskar felt the two players were spared a potentially awkward situation, including the prospect of facing criticism from fans on social media if India had delayed sealing the victory to give Kohli a chance to complete his hundred."Kohli got out in the 70s. Gill and Iyer were thus spared any blowback if the winning runs had been hit with Kohli unbeaten in the 90s. Yes, it's a team game, but it's also good for the team if one of its members, especially a star player, gets to a personal milestone without affecting the team's chances of winning," Gavaskar pointed out.Kohli, who now plays only ODIs, has 86 international centuries to his name. He is chasing a landmark that remains exclusive to Sachin Tendulkar, the only batter to have scored 100 international hundreds.

Article Title: ‘He got greedy’: Ex-India captain's blunt take on Arshdeep Singh after four-wicket haul
Article Text:

Former India cricketer Ajay Jadeja has praised Arshdeep Singh's overall performance in India's five-wicket victory over New Zealand in the first ODI in Auckland, but believes the left-arm pacer could have avoided an expensive finish to his spell.India began their five-match ODI series with a comfortable win at Eden Park on Wednesday, November 4. In a rain-interrupted contest reduced to 32 overs per side, New Zealand were bowled out for 185 before India chased down the revised target of 143 in just 22.4 overs. Virat Kohli led the chase with a fluent 74, while Shubman Gill contributed 37 as the duo stitched together a 113-run partnership. India eventually crossed the finish line with five wickets to spare and 56 deliveries remaining.With the ball, Arshdeep was India's leading wicket-taker, claiming four wickets in his 10 overs. However, his figures of 4/70 were inflated by an expensive final over in which New Zealand tailender Blair Tickner struck him for three sixes, taking 23 runs off the over.Assessing the pacer's performance, Jadeja felt Arshdeep had been impressive for most of his spell but allowed the opportunity to complete a five-wicket haul to influence his bowling towards the end."I would call him slightly greedy. He himself said that as well. If you remove his last over, he had dismissed four batters before that and had given 40-odd runs. He got slightly greedy for the fifth wicket in the last over," Jadeja said on Sony Sports Network.Arshdeep had himself admitted after the match that the fifth wicket would have been his favourite, indicating that he was keen to complete a five-wicket haul. Despite missing out on the milestone, his four-wicket effort placed him in an exclusive group of Indian fast bowlers to achieve the feat in an ODI in New Zealand, alongside Javagal Srinath and Mohammed Shami.Jadeja, however, stressed that the expensive final over should not overshadow what Arshdeep brings to India's bowling combination. He pointed to the value of having a left-arm fast bowler in an attack that already features Jasprit Bumrah, adding that the competition for places would only benefit the team."It happens. It's natural, but Arshdeep Singh is showing that he can play in ODIs as well, which I believe is a very good thing when a left-arm seamer gets added to this attack with (Jasprit) Bumrah. The competition has increased a lot, which is very good for India," Jadeja elaborated.Jadeja also reserved praise for Anshul Kamboj, who delivered an economical spell of 2/22 from his 10 overs and walked away with the Player of the Match award.The former India batter acknowledged that Kamboj had faced questions over his bowling during his Test debut against England in 2025, particularly regarding his pace and tendency to bowl no-balls. However, he felt the youngster had shown considerable improvement in Auckland.Jadeja also suggested that Kamboj's workload before the England assignment could have contributed to his struggles, pointing out that fatigue can affect a bowler's execution. His performance against New Zealand, according to Jadeja, reflected better pace, consistency and accuracy."He bowled extremely well. The vision everyone had was that he didn't have pace when he played in England and was bowling a lot of no-balls. I think he had come after playing a lot of cricket then. So a guy also gets tired. It's not that easy. Then he was playing for the first time, but the consistency and the slight increase in his pace he showed today (Wednesday), if we talk about the accuracy amongst the four bowlers, it's Anshul Kamboj," Jadeja added.
Article Summary: India beat New Zealand by five wickets in the first ODI in Auckland. Ajay Jadeja praised Arshdeep Singh's performance, but said he could have avoided expensive final over. Jadeja also praised Anshul Kamboj's bowling, saying he had shown improvement.

Article Title: 'Mate, well done': Australia captain Mitch Marsh responds to Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering claims
Article Text:
Usman Khawaja

What happened in the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal?

Australia captain Mitch Marsh chose not to discuss the Sandpapergate scandal on Thursday, saying his focus was on leading the team in the upcoming white-ball series against England rather than revisiting events in Cape Town eight years ago.Marsh faced the media in Perth, five days after former Australia teammate Usman Khawaja brought the ball-tampering controversy back into the spotlight. In his autobiography, Khawaja claimed that the entire Australian squad knew about the plan to use sandpaper to rough up the ball during the 2018 Test against South Africa.The incident led to lengthy bans for three Australian players and had a major impact on cricket in the country. In the eight years since, Cricket Australia, the team management and several players have rarely spoken about the controversy. Members of Australia's bowling group have rejected claims that the entire team knew about the plan to use sandpaper to help the ball swing through the air.When asked about the scandal at the start of his scheduled press conference, Marsh responded: “You hit a six off the first ball there, Mate, well done!” He then added: “Look, obviously there's been a bit of noise around this week and I respect that certain people have told their stories."“I'm not here to share mine today, I know that might sound weird, but it's a big week for us and it's an important time for this one-day (squad) and my sole focus has been on preparing for tomorrow.”The controversy has dominated cricket coverage this week and is expected to remain a talking point as the Australian summer gets underway.Australia and England begin their white-ball series in Perth on Friday, with three ODIs and five T20Is scheduled between the teams. Meanwhile, Australia Test captain Pat Cummins is set to address the controversy at a press conference in Sydney, hours before the opening match.Cummins said he had taken time to understand Khawaja's claims before responding. “Happy to speak with any and all media about the events of this week,” Cummins posted on X. “I've taken some time to try and better understand the long list and full extent of Uzzy's allegations so I can respond properly.”Steve Smith and David Warner, who were Australia's captain and vice-captain at the time, were each handed 12-month bans by Cricket Australia following an investigation into the ball-tampering incident. Cameron Bancroft, who was caught using sandpaper on the ball during the Test match, received a nine-month ban.Smith and Warner returned to the Australian team in 2019. Smith continues to play Test cricket for the country and is preparing for a four-match series against New Zealand starting next month.
Article Summary: Australia captain Mitch Marsh chose not to discuss the Sandpapergate scandal. Marsh said his focus was on leading the team in the upcoming white-ball series against England. The incident led to lengthy bans for three Australian players and had a major impact on cricket.

New Zealand's batters have found little room to breathe against India's disciplined pace attack, and Tim Seifert believes the biggest challenge has been the visitors' ability to operate as a unit rather than rely on one standout bowler.With India leading the five-match ODI series 2-0, the New Zealand wicketkeeper-batter admitted his side could not identify a particular Indian bowler to target, crediting the variety and consistency within the attack for putting the hosts under pressure.India's pace battery, featuring Arshdeep Singh , Anshul Kamboj, Auqib Nabi and Gurnoor Brar, has troubled New Zealand in the first two matches. Gurnoor has emerged as the leading wicket-taker in the series with seven scalps, while the third ODI in Hamilton was abandoned without a ball being bowled due to rain.Seifert pointed to the different qualities each Indian pacer brings to the attack, particularly highlighting the advantage of having a left-arm option in Arshdeep."They all bowl very well, they all do something slightly different. Having Arshdeep (Singh) as a left-hander, I think it's crucial as well. But to be honest, they work well as a unit. They all do something a little bit different," Seifert said during the pre-match press conference."To their credit, they didn't miss much on those wickets the last two games. I can't really target anyone individually; I think they do a very good job together," he added.Despite the results not going their way, Seifert said New Zealand had faced challenging batting conditions and were focused on making the most of the remaining two matches. The hosts have also undergone changes in personnel, with several players leaving the ODI squad to prepare for the upcoming Test series, which begins on November 19."It's good. I think, look, obviously the result hasn't necessarily gone our way, but we've obviously been put in some tricky situations with the wickets as well. So, look, it's a new bunch of guys here. A few guys have left for the Test series starting on November 19, so we're just focusing on the next two games ahead," he said.Asked about the changes in personnel in both camps, Seifert said the challenge remained the same regardless of who featured in the playing XI. He insisted that every player coming into the side would be an international cricketer capable of making an impact, adding that New Zealand would approach the final two matches with the same competitive mindset."No matter who India play or whoever we play as well, we're out there for the challenge, and everyone's an international cricketer out there. So whoever steps into their role, they're going to try their best. Same with us, whoever steps into the role that the boys have left, everyone's going to try their best as well," he concluded.

Article Title: 21 sixes in an innings! New Zealand batter Bevon Jacobs comes close to world record

From India series to domestic record

New Zealand batter Bevon Jacobs produced a stunning batting display in the domestic Ford Trophy on Thursday, smashing an unbeaten 202 off just 137 balls against Otago in Auckland.The 21 sixes in his innings set a new record for the most sixes hit by a New Zealand batter in a List A innings. Jacobs was just two sixes short of the world record of 23, held by Australia's Da’Arcy Short.His powerful knock helped Auckland post 334/8 at the Kennards Hire Community Oval. However, Jacobs' effort went in vain as Otago chased down the target in 49.1 overs.A total of 34 sixes were hit in the match.Batting at No. 4, Jacobs turned his maiden List A century into a double century with some powerful hitting. He reached the 200-run mark in just 137 balls, hitting seven fours and 21 sixes.The 21 sixes are the most by a New Zealand batter in a List A innings. Jacobs came close to breaking the world record, which belongs to Australia's Da’Arcy Short. Short had hit 23 sixes while scoring 257 off 148 balls for Western Australia against Queensland in Sydney in 2018.Jacobs also became only the fourth New Zealand batter to score a double century in List A cricket. He joined Jamie How (2012), Martin Guptill (2015) and Chad Bowes (2024) on the list.His 202 not out was also a record score for Auckland Aces in the Ford Trophy and the third double century in the tournament's history.Jacobs recently featured in New Zealand's five-match T20I series against India. He scored more than 135 runs against the world champions and followed it up with this remarkable performance in domestic cricket.The 28-year-old has also played 16 T20Is for New Zealand since making his debut in late 2024. However, he is yet to make his debut in ODIs and Test cricket.
Article Summary: Bevon Jacobs hits 21 sixes in record-breaking knock for Auckland Aces. Jacobs comes close to breaking world record of 23 set by Australia's Da’Arcy Short. Jacobs becomes only fourth New Zealand batter to score a double century in List A cricket.

Article Title: 'We absolutely support Pat': Cricket Australia backs Cummins amid fresh Sandpapergate row
Article Text:
Pat Cummins (AFP Photo)

Boon says Cricket Australia has full faith in Cummins

Warner and Sayers support Khawaja's version

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Hick and Starc deny prior knowledge

Cricket Australia chairman David Boon has thrown his support behind Test captain Pat Cummins following fresh allegations about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal. Boon has made it clear that Cummins' position as captain is safe and that the board continues to have full faith in him.The controversy has returned to the spotlight after former Australia batter Usman Khawaja made fresh claims in his autobiography, "Sabr". Khawaja alleged that all members of the Australian team on the 2018 South Africa tour knew about the plan to tamper with the ball.His claims have reopened the debate over the scandal and led to demands for another investigation. Cummins, who now leads Australia's Test team, has also come under pressure to explain what he knew.Boon said Cummins had led the team with honesty and had the board's complete backing.“We absolutely support Pat,” Boon said in comments published by The Australian on Thursday.“He’s been an exemplary captain, he’s led the team with integrity and, you know, very successfully over the period of time that he’s been captain, so there’s no question of our confidence in him continuing on in that fact.”Cummins has not yet publicly addressed Khawaja's allegations.He, however, posted on X that he would speak to the media on Friday after going through the claims."I've taken some time to try and better understand the long list and full extent of Uzzy's allegations so I can respond properly," he wrote.Mitchell Marsh , Australia's white-ball captain, is also expected to address the issue. Marsh was part of the Test team during the 2018 tour and will speak at a press conference in Perth later on Thursday, ahead of the ODI against England.Khawaja's claims have received support from former teammate David Warner . Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft were all banned for their roles in the ball-tampering scandal.Former Australia fast bowler Chadd Sayers, who was also part of the 2018 South Africa tour, has also backed Khawaja. Speaking to Australian media last weekend, Sayers said the allegations were "accurate".Despite the fresh claims, Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg said on Tuesday that there was no compelling reason to reopen the investigation.Boon repeated the same position, saying the board did not want to get into a dispute over different versions of events."I respect (Usman’s) point of view and his recollections of what occurred, and they’re his, but we don’t want to get into a he-said-she-said argument," he said."There are going to be supporters, there’s going to be other guys that don’t recollect the same thing, so I don’t see a purpose.”In his book "Sabr", released this week, Khawaja claimed that Australia had tampered with the ball during the second Test in South Africa as well, and not just in the third Test in Cape Town.Former Australia batting coach Graeme Hick has strongly rejected the claims, calling them "absolutely false"."In regard to any discussions around the ball-tampering in Port Elizabeth or Cape Town that took place, I will say in true honesty that I did not hear or know anything," he told the Sydney Morning Herald.Fast bowler Mitchell Starc has also denied having prior knowledge of the ball-tampering.In 2021, Starc and fellow bowlers Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon issued a joint statement. They said they did not know that a "foreign substance" had been taken onto the field to tamper with the ball during the Cape Town Test.
Article Summary: Cricket Australia chairman David Boon backs Test captain Pat Cummins. Boon says board has full faith in Cummins following fresh ball-tampering claims. Former Australia batter Usman Khawaja made fresh claims in his autobiography, "Sabr" Former teammate David Warner and former fast bowler Chadd Sayers also support Khawja's claims.

NEW DELHI: New Zealand have added a record-breaking fast bowler Brett Randell to their squad for the remaining two ODIs against India. Randell made history earlier this year by becoming the first bowler in the 254-year history of first-class cricket to take five wickets in five balls.The 31-year-old has been included in the squad for the fourth and fifth ODIs against India. He is also in line to make his international debut in the fourth match, which will be played on Friday.India lead the five-match series 2-0 after winning the first two games. The third ODI in Hamilton was abandoned due to rain.Randell has played 145 professional matches, including five for New Zealand A. He recently returned from a stint with English county side Derbyshire in the County Championship.New Zealand Cricket has also added all-rounder Josh Clarkson to the squad for the fifth and final ODI, scheduled for Sunday.Randell created history while playing for Central Stags against Northern Districts in New Zealand's Plunket Shield in March this year. The 31-year-old took five wickets in five consecutive balls on the second day of the match, becoming the first bowler in the 254-year history of first-class cricket to achieve the feat.While Randell was the first to do it in first-class cricket, five wickets in five balls had been achieved in other formats before.Ireland's Curtis Campher became the first male player to take five wickets in five balls in a professional match during a domestic T20 game in July 2025.Zimbabwe Women all-rounder Kelis Ndhlovu had also achieved the feat in a domestic Under-19 T20 match in 2024.New Zealand head coach Rob Walter congratulated Randell on his first international call-up and praised his consistent performances in domestic cricket."It's always a special time when a player earns their first international call up," said Walter."We're very pleased for Brett, he's been a consistent performer in domestic cricket for some time now and has earned this opportunity. I think we are almost there. Hardik brings that Midas touch to us.No puzzle is ever perfectly complete. All the players have to come together and perform well. But I think, as a collective group under the leadership of Shreyas and Ricky, we have proved that we can stand up and deliver.We reached the final in 2025, and were doing really well in 2026, before slipping up towards the end. I think that was down to a lack of experience. Sometimes, overconfidence also creeps in. There were also players who did not perform at their expected levels. But we certainly have the potential to win not just one, but several championships. That is the objective for Hardik, Shreyas, Ricky and all of us.The league has to keep evolving. I think it is good that the trading window was introduced and that it remains open even after the retention deadline. It is interesting because a lot of trades have happened this year.It shows that franchises are willing to make difficult calls, go into an auction, do the best they can and then assess how things work out over the next one or two years. They can subsequently make adjustments and tweak their squads. But as far as we are concerned, we are looking at Hardik as a long-term investment, not just a short-term move.You never know. Stranger things have happened! We still have few days left, so a lot can happen in that time. These things can move very quickly.Of course, if a trade is on the cards, franchises can always agree and complete it even after the retention deadline. That is the beauty of having the trading window open after retentions as well.As far as the IPL window is concerned, it would be good to have a different window because, with changing weather patterns, it sometimes starts raining or gets very hot, making conditions difficult for players. Ideally, one could look at shifting the tournament.However, we will have to consider the domestic and international cricket calendars and see what is possible. But it is certainly something worth exploring.It is difficult. It is difficult for the players as well. But we have to look at the bigger picture. At the end of the day, it is also about the revenue we generate and the support we receive from both Punjab Cricket Association (PCA) and Himachal Pradesh Cricket Association (HPCA). It would be fantastic if that support continues. Let's see how things develop going forward. Having said that, these are world-class players, and everyone adjusts and adapts. You can look at it as having one additional venue.

Article Title: Best ever! From 14 medals to 114: How India achieved more with fewer athletes at the Asian Para Games
Article Text:

From 14 medals to 114: India's remarkable rise

India's Asian Para Games record

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Smaller contingent, bigger return

Hangzhou vs Aichi-Nagoya

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Athletics powers India's medal surge

India's leading medal-winning sports in Asian Para Games 2026

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Multiple medallists underline India's depth

Paralympic progress provides the wider context

Fourth place sets a new benchmark

From 14 medals in 2010 to 114 in 2026, India’s remarkable rise continued in Aichi-Nagoya as a smaller contingent surpassed its previous best, achieved 30 gold medals and secured its highest-ever finish at the continental para-sport showpiece.India’s campaign at the Asian Para Games 2026 was a triumph that few would have predicted when the size of the contingent became known. With just 167 athletes travelling to Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, the prospect of repeating the 100-plus medal haul achieved at Hangzhou in 2023 appeared ambitious. The previous edition had seen India send more than 300 athletes to the competition, returning with a record 108 medals after subsequent revisions to the original tally.But the Indian contingent defied expectations, producing an even bigger return with significantly fewer athletes. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place, both the highest medal tally and the best finish in the country's history at the event.The numbers tell a compelling story of progress. India improved its medal tally for the fifth consecutive edition, added to its gold-medal record and finished ahead of South Korea, which had threatened to challenge its position in the final standings.More than the record itself, the achievement highlighted how far India's para-sport movement has travelled in 16 years — from a modest 14-medal return at the inaugural edition in 2010 to a fourth-place finish among Asia's leading para-sport nations.India's progress at the Asian Para Games has been steady, with each edition bringing a new high in the overall medal tally.At Guangzhou in 2010, India won 14 medals — one gold, four silver and nine bronze — to finish 15th. The 2014 edition in Incheon brought a substantial improvement, with the country collecting 33 medals, including three gold, but remaining 15th in the standings.The breakthrough arrived at Jakarta in 2018. India's medal tally rose to 72, comprising 15 gold, 24 silver and 33 bronze, while its position improved to ninth.Hangzhou in 2023 marked another major leap. India crossed the 100-medal barrier for the first time, initially returning with 111 medals before the tally was revised to 108 following a doping-related disqualification and a medal reallocation. The revised haul comprised 27 gold, 32 silver and 49 bronze, with India eventually classified sixth.Aichi-Nagoya extended that upward trajectory. India added six medals to its revised Hangzhou total, increased its gold-medal count from 27 to 30 and climbed two places to fourth.The numbers at a glance: India's medal tally increased more than eightfold between 2010 and 2026. Its gold-medal count grew from one to 30, while its position improved from 15th to fourth.The rise has not been limited to the overall tally. India has improved its standing in three successive editions since 2014, moving from 15th to ninth, then sixth and now fourth. The 2026 result represents the culmination of a sustained upward trend rather than an isolated breakthrough.The most striking feature of India's latest performance was the efficiency with which its athletes converted participation into medals.India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi-Nagoya. That was considerably fewer than the 309 athletes listed for the Hangzhou campaign in 2023, yet the team surpassed its previous best by six medals.The comparison is revealing. India sent approximately 46 per cent fewer athletes than it did to Hangzhou, but its medal tally increased by nearly six per cent. The gold-medal count rose by three, the silver tally by three, and the bronze count remained unchanged.On a simple medals-per-athlete measure, India's return increased from approximately 0.35 medals per athlete in Hangzhou to 0.68 in Aichi-Nagoya. This is an aggregate comparison, not an individual success rate, since athletes can win multiple medals and the number of events and opportunities varies across sports.Nevertheless, the figures underline the scale of the achievement. A smaller squad did not merely match the previous edition's success; it established a new benchmark for Indian para-sport.Para-athletics was the backbone of India's campaign, delivering 65 medals — 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. That represented nearly 57 per cent of the country's overall tally and made athletics the single biggest contributor to India's fourth-place finish.Para-badminton followed with 16 medals, including three gold, five silver and eight bronze. Together, athletics and badminton accounted for 81 medals, more than 70 per cent of India's total.Swimming contributed 11 medals, comprising three silver and eight bronze. Archery added six medals, including three gold and three silver, while shooting produced five, with two gold, two silver and one bronze.Athletics' contribution also illustrates how India's progress has accelerated. At Hangzhou, para-athletics produced 52 medals, including 16 gold, 17 silver and 19 bronze. In Aichi-Nagoya, the discipline's haul rose to 65, with six additional gold medals.Badminton's contribution was different. India won 21 medals in the sport at Hangzhou, including four gold, but finished with 16 in 2026. Instead, the substantial gains in athletics and the contributions from other sports helped compensate for the decline in badminton medals.That distinction matters: the record haul reflects both the strength of India's established medal-winning disciplines and the need to broaden its success across events in future editions.India's record was supported by athletes who delivered more than once during the competition. A total of 26 Indian athletes won multiple medals, while six athletes collected multiple gold medals, demonstrating the importance of individual excellence in a campaign involving 11 sports.Archer Sheetal Devi was among the standout performers, winning two gold medals and a silver. Her two golds came in the mixed compound and individual compound events, while the silver added to her three-medal haul.Athletics provided several other multiple gold medallists. Dilip Gavit, Nishad Kumar, Pranav Soorma and Simran Sharma each won two gold medals, while shooting contributed through Mona Agarwal, who also secured two golds.Four athletes finished with three medals apiece: Sheetal Devi in archery, Thulasimathi Murugesan in badminton, Ravi Budigina in swimming and Himanshu Nandal in swimming. Their performances illustrated how athletes winning across multiple events can make a significant difference to a country's final tally.The figures also invite comparison with Hangzhou, where 25 Indian athletes won multiple medals. The increase to 26 in 2026 was modest, but the overall tally improved despite a much smaller contingent. The result points to a campaign in which medal-winning performances were concentrated among a relatively small squad.India's rise at the Asian Para Games has coincided with a significant improvement at the Paralympics, strengthening the country's standing in international para-sport.At Rio 2016, India won four medals and finished 43rd. Tokyo 2020 marked a breakthrough, with 19 medals — five gold, eight silver and six bronze — lifting India to 24th. At Paris 2024, India recorded its best Paralympic haul of 29 medals, comprising seven gold, nine silver and 13 bronze, to finish 18th.The progression at the Paralympics mirrors the broader trend at the Asian Para Games: larger medal returns, more gold medals and improvements in the standings.India's able-bodied contingent had also finished fourth at the 2026 Asian Games, although its 85-medal tally was below the 106 medals achieved at Hangzhou in 2023. The para contingent's performance offered a contrasting story of growth, with its medal count rising and its position improving.China dominated Aichi-Nagoya, finishing with 435 medals, including 207 gold. Hosts Japan were second with 186 medals, while Uzbekistan finished third with 145. India placed fourth with 114, ahead of South Korea, which collected 100 medals, including 29 gold.India's final position was not guaranteed until the closing stages. South Korea remained within reach, but its final-day return of one gold and two silver left it one gold behind India. The Indian contingent held on to fourth place with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze.The gap to third-placed Uzbekistan shows that further progress will require India to expand its medal-winning strength across disciplines. Yet the immediate achievement is significant: India has moved from 15th at the first two editions to fourth, while increasing its tally at every successive Games.The challenge now is to sustain that momentum, build a deeper pool of competitive athletes and reduce dependence on a handful of disciplines.For a contingent of just 167 athletes, 114 medals represent more than a record. They mark the latest step in a 16-year transformation of Indian para-sport — one that began with 14 medals in Guangzhou and has now culminated in a historic fourth-place finish in Aichi-Nagoya.
Article Summary: India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi- Nagoya. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place. It is the best finish in the country's history at the event.

Article Text:

Third Paralympics, one big dream: Gold at LA 2028

IAS officer by day, shuttler by night

NEW DELHI: Suhas Yathiraj was disappointed with his bronze medal at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya. Having beaten Indonesia's Fredy Setiawan in their group match just days earlier, the Indian shuttler had hoped to reach the final and fight for gold.Suhas lost the men's singles SL4 semifinal 23-21, 8-21, 15-21. He had chances to take the opening game but failed to convert them. After bouncing back to win the second game 21-8, he lost focus at a crucial stage of the decider.“Definitely not satisfied with bronze. I think if I had played up to my full potential, I would have definitely done better. In fact, I defeated Fredy of Indonesia in the group match in Nagoya only a few days ago,” Suhas told TimesofIndia.com from Aichi-Nagoya in Japan.“In the semifinal match, the first set was very close. I lost 23-21 and I had game point, set point, but I couldn't convert that. In the second set, I won very easily. In the third set, I think after 10-all, I sort of lost focus for two to three rallies. That is where he took the game. So, it was not my best day, I would assume. I would always love to win a gold medal. So, yes, I am a little sad from that angle,” he said.The defeat also reminded him of how important it is to perform under pressure at major tournaments.“It is the most important factor to win medals at major games because you might be training well, you might actually have the fitness and the skills. But if you don't recreate that during the major games, then probably it is of not much use in terms of professional success,” Suhas said.Suhas, an IAS officer, said he had never imagined representing India in international badminton a decade ago.In November 2016, he made his debut at the Asian Championships in Beijing and won gold. Since then, he has won several medals at major international events. These include bronze at the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, silver at the Tokyo 2020 Paralympics, another silver at the Paris 2024 Paralympics, gold at the Hangzhou Asian Para Games and bronze in Nagoya.The 43-year-old has represented India at two Paralympic Games, Tokyo in 2020 and Paris in 2024, winning silver on both occasions.With the Los Angeles 2028 Paralympics approaching, the big question is whether he can go one step further and win gold.The desire is there, but Suhas is not looking too far ahead. He wants to take things one step at a time.“If you had asked me 10 years ago, I didn't even know that I would play for India. But whenever I look at the medals and the love I have got from fans and sportspersons around the world, the journey has been quite satisfying. I have had the honour of wearing the Indian jersey and winning medals for my country,” he said.“I am grateful for what God has given me. I never imagined that I would become an IAS officer one day, an Arjuna awardee or a badminton player winning medals for India. I never imagined all this. But thanks to the Almighty for all these,” Suhas, who is also an Arjuna Award recipient, said.“So if God and destiny have been kind to me, I hope they will take me to a place that I deserve. I hope I can do the best that I can in whatever I choose to,” he added.For most people, the end of a hectic working day is a time to relax, spend time with family, play with their children or watch a movie.For Suhas, it is often time to pick up his badminton racket and head to the court. His day includes early-morning gym sessions, office work, inspections, meetings, video conferences and checking files. Despite his demanding responsibilities as an IAS officer, he makes time for badminton and follows a strict fitness routine to compete at the highest level.Balancing the two careers is not easy, but his love for the sport keeps him going.“If you choose what you love, then the journey becomes painless. You enjoy that journey. That's what I do,” Suhas said.Explaining how he manages his work and training, he said: “It is challenging. My training generally starts in the night and it always involves sacrifices. Probably others would be spending time with their family members or having leisure time. My leisure time is to play badminton. In badminton, you need an extremely high level of fitness. It's challenging, hectic but at the same time I love it.”“I don't remember eating sweets in the last many months. I can't recall when I had my last sweet. So, I almost don't eat sweets or fried food and am also quite conscious about the nutrition that I take,” he said.Suhas grew up watching Malaysian badminton great Lee Chong Wei and was inspired by his movement on the court.“Yes, I have always been inspired by so many top players in the able-bodied category. Growing up, I watched the matches of Lee Chong Wei and how he used to move around the court,” he said.“Even in India, the top shuttlers perform extremely well, whether it is Lakshya Sen, HS Prannoy or Kidambi Srikanth. I know them personally and have always admired how well they are able to compete at the top,” Suhas signed off.
Article Summary: Suhas Yathiraj was disappointed with his bronze medal at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya. The Indian shuttler lost the men's singles SL4 semifinal 23- 21, 8-21, 15-21. Suhas has represented India at two Paralympic Games, Tokyo in 2020 and Paris in 2024.

The country's final tally of 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze surpassed its previous best of 108 medals, including 27 gold, achieved at the Hangzhou Games in 2023.The achievement was particularly significant as India competed with a contingent of 168 athletes, nearly half the size of the squad that represented the country in Hangzhou.India remained fourth in the standings at the end of its campaign, although the final positions could change after a few remaining events on Saturday.Athletics remained India's biggest medal contributor, accounting for 65 medals, 12 more than at the previous edition. On Friday, however, the spotlight was shared with a superb badminton campaign and gold-winning performances in shooting and archery. Star javelin thrower Sumit Antil led an Indian 1-2-3 finish in the men's F42-44/61-64 combined event . The reigning Paralympic and world champion threw 72.46m to defend his title, while Mahendra Gurjar took silver with 59.03m and Sandip Sanjay Sargar claimed bronze with 64.48m. Gurjar finished ahead of Sargar on Raza points, which determine rankings in combined-classification events.Pranav Soorma added another gold in the men's club throw F51, defending his title with a Games-record effort of 32.87m. Dharambir secured bronze with 27.71m.Sandeep delivered a world-record performance in the men's 400m T64, clocking 52.28 seconds for gold. India also picked up silver medals through Nimisha Chakkungalparambil in the women's long jump T47 and Parmod Bijarnia in the men's 1500m T46, where he clocked 4:09.65.India's badminton contingent delivered three gold medals, led by Paris Paralympic champion Nitesh Kumar and Games debutant Naveen Sivakumar.Nitesh defeated compatriot and Tokyo Paralympic gold medallist Pramod Bhagat 21-18, 21-16 in the men's singles SL3 final. He later added a silver medal in mixed doubles SL3-SU5 alongside Thulasimathi Murugesan.Naveen, meanwhile, defeated Indonesia's Fredy Setiawan 21-9, 21-17 to win the men's singles SL4 title. Thulasimathi enjoyed a memorable campaign of her own , combining with Manasi Joshi to win gold in women's doubles SL3-SU5. The Indian pair beat China's Yang Qiuxia and Xiao Zuxian 21-16, 21-13 in the final.The 24-year-old also secured silver in women's singles SU5 after losing 18-21, 11-21 to Yang in the final, completing a three-medal haul.Shooter Mona Agarwal added another golden chapter to India's campaign, shattering the world record to win the women's 50m rifle 3 positions SH1 title with a score of 357.5 points.The 38-year-old had earlier won the women's 10m air rifle standing SH1 gold with a Games-record score of 250.0 points, edging compatriot Avani Lekhara, who took silver with 249.6.Mona's latest triumph gave her a second gold of the Games and further underlined her standing among India's leading para-shooters. She had also secured India's first 2028 Paralympic quota earlier this year.In archery, Paralympic champion Harvinder Singh teamed up with debutant Vijay Sundi to win the men's recurve doubles gold, defeating China's Yun Duo and Zhao Lixue 5-1 in the final.India's women's recurve doubles pair of Bhawna Choudhary and Pooja Jatyan settled for silver after losing 0-6 to China's Gao Zihan and Wang Xueqian.India's swimmers also exceeded expectations, finishing the Games with 11 medals, including three silver. The 22-year-old, who was born blind due to optic nerve failure, clocked 1:05.90, behind Japan's Uchu Tomita (58.22) and China's Chuanzhen Sun (58.70).Nandal had earlier won bronze in the men's 400m freestyle and 100m breaststroke S11 events. NEW DELHI: Indian para-swimmer Himanshu Nandal made his mark at the Asian Para Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, completing a hat-trick of bronze medals with another podium finish in the men's 100m freestyle S11 event on Friday.The 22-year-old clocked 1 minute 5.90 seconds to finish third, behind Japan's Uchu Tomita, who won gold in a Games-record time of 58.22 seconds, and China's Chuanzhen Sun, who took silver in 58.70 seconds.Nandal's latest medal added to his earlier bronze finishes in the men's 400m freestyle and 100m breaststroke S11 events. Article Title: War fears reach the football: US withdraw from FIFA U-17 World Cup in Qatar over security concerns
Article Text:

The United States has withdrawn from the upcoming Under-17 FIFA World Cup in Qatar over security concerns in the Middle East, according to US media reports on Wednesday.The decision was communicated to the players just over a week before the tournament begins on November 19, US Soccer Collective and The Athletic reported.US Soccer, the governing body of the sport in the United States, has not officially confirmed the withdrawal, news agency AFP reported.The decision comes amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which began in February with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran. Tehran retaliated by targeting several locations, including Gulf countries allied with Washington.Diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have continued, but the United States and Israel have repeatedly threatened to resume strikes on Iran.The conflict has also affected several sporting events in the region. The WTA Finals, which were scheduled to take place in Saudi Arabia, Qatar's neighbour, have been shifted to Indian Wells in the United States.This season's Formula One Grand Prix in Jeddah was cancelled, while the Bahrain race was also called off and later rescheduled under the same name in Malaysia. Several sporting events in Saudi Arabia have also been cancelled or postponed in recent weeks following attacks on the country by Yemen's Houthis.The United States were among the 48 teams scheduled to compete in the Under-17 World Cup. They had been placed in a group alongside Montenegro, Chile and Algeria.The Under-17 World Cup became an annual tournament last year and is being hosted by Qatar for five consecutive editions.When FIFA announced Qatar as the host for these tournaments in 2024, it said the decision to have one country host multiple editions was based on the opportunity to make "use of existing footballing infrastructure in the interest of tournament efficiencies and sustainability".Qatar had earlier hosted the 2022 men's FIFA World Cup.
Article Summary: The United States have withdrawn from the upcoming Under-17 FIFA World Cup in Qatar over security concerns in the Middle East. The decision was communicated to the players just over a week before the tournament begins on November 19. US Soccer, the governing body of the sport in the United States, has not officially confirmed the withdrawal.

France have suffered a major setback ahead of their crucial UEFA Nations League encounter against Italy, with captain Kylian Mbappe missing training due to a hamstring issue. Les Bleus currently lead their group and can secure their place in the last eight with a victory over Italy.
